common_name: BabyWing White Begonia (Compact Orchid-Flowered Interspecific Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade or sun; BabyWing White is a compact interspecific hybrid begonia bearing large, orchid-like white flowers on a tidy 12-15 inch plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade or sun, watering to keep soil evenly moist without becoming soggy. BabyWing White, an interspecific hybrid bred by PanAmerican Seed, bears unusually large, pure white, orchid-like flowers held above glossy dark green foliage on a compact, well-branched plant, a smaller-scale growth habit than the taller Whopper and Dragon Wing hybrid begonias in the same interspecific group. It blooms nonstop from planting through frost with no deadheading required, holding up well to summer heat and humidity, and performs equally well in a shaded bed, a partly sunny border, or a container. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only regular watering during dry spells; treat as an annual outside its tender perennial zone range.

common_name: Kauai Rose Wishbone Flower (Compact Early-Blooming Bicolor Torenia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kauai Rose is a compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant wishbone flower bred for hand-painted bicolor rose-and-yellow blooms.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil consistently moist through the heat of summer. Kauai Rose is part of a compact, early-flowering wishbone flower series bred for uniform, hand-painted bicolor blooms combining rich rose-pink outer petals with a bright yellow throat, held on a tidy, mounding plant that begins flowering earlier in the season than older torenia strains. It thrives in the shaded conditions where many other flowering annuals struggle, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with excellent heat and humidity tolerance, making it a reliable Gulf South shade bedding and container annual. No deadheading is required to keep it flowering. Water regularly during dry spells, since consistent moisture keeps the display at its best.

common_name: Silver Bells Browallia (White-Flowered Bush Violet for Shade)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Silver Bells bears pure white flowers, a bright counterpart to the blue-toned Browallia cultivars more commonly grown.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, watering regularly to keep soil consistently moist. Silver Bells bears an abundance of star-shaped, pure white flowers on a compact, mounding plant, a bright, clean color option among browallia cultivars that are more typically bred in shades of blue and violet, brightening dark corners of the shade garden or a shaded container planting. It blooms continuously from planting through frost without deadheading, tolerating heat and humidity well, and is one of the true shade-loving flowering annuals, performing better in shade than in full sun where the foliage can scorch. Treat as a warm-season annual outside its tender perennial zone range, and pinch stems occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier habit.

common_name: Stained Glassworks Royalty Coleus (Large Mottled Deep-Shade Stained-Glass-Pattern Coleus)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Royalty, part of the Stained Glassworks series bred specifically for deep shade, bears large, mottled leaves patterned like stained glass.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Stained Glassworks series was bred specifically to hold strong foliage color and pattern in deeper shade than most coleus cultivars tolerate without fading or stretching. Royalty bears large, bold leaves marked in a rich, mottled pattern of deep purple, burgundy, and green blocked together like the leaded panes of a stained-glass window, a dramatic, large-scale foliage effect that reads well even from a distance in a shaded bed or large container. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage a fuller, bushier habit and remove flower spikes as they form, since coleus declines in vigor once it sets seed. Treat as a warm-season annual outside its tender perennial zone range, or take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors.

common_name: SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender New Guinea Impatiens (Large Vase-Habit Downy-Mildew-Resistant Impatiens)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender is the large-form, vase-habit tier of the SunPatiens line, reaching 30-36 inches, with strong resistance to downy mildew.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, watering regularly to keep soil consistently moist. SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender is the largest-growing tier of the SunPatiens breeding line, forming a substantial, upright, vase-shaped plant 30 to 36 inches tall covered in soft lavender-pink flowers from spring through frost, a dramatically bigger scale than the compact, mounding SunPatiens forms bred for smaller beds and containers. Like the rest of the SunPatiens line, it carries strong resistance to the downy mildew that devastated old-fashioned impatiens walleriana plantings, and tolerates considerably more sun than traditional shade impatiens while still performing well in partial shade. Its size makes it useful as a substantial seasonal hedge, back-of-border filler, or large container centerpiece. No deadheading is needed to keep it blooming continuously.

common_name: Autumn Jazz Arrowwood Viburnum (Uniform Reliable Fall-Color Native Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Jazz, a Chicagoland Grows selection of native arrowwood viburnum, bears a dense, uniform habit and reliable red-orange to yellow fall color, with blue-black berries that are heavily favored by birds.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native arrowwood viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and light conditions. Autumn Jazz, a Chicagoland Grows introduction, is a selection of native arrowwood viburnum bred for a dense, uniform, rounded habit and unusually reliable fall foliage color, turning a consistent blend of red-orange to burgundy each autumn rather than the more variable coloring typical of seedling-grown arrowwood. Flat clusters of white spring flowers give way to blue-black berries in fall that are heavily favored by migrating and overwintering songbirds, making it a valuable native wildlife planting as well as an ornamental hedge or screen. It requires minimal maintenance once established and tolerates urban conditions, clay soil, and periodic drought well. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Chicago Lustre Arrowwood Viburnum (Glossy Disease-Resistant Heavy-Fruiting Native Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chicago Lustre bears glossy, dark green, disease-resistant foliage and heavier-than-typical fruit set, providing abundant food for birds.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native arrowwood viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and light conditions. Chicago Lustre is a selection of native arrowwood viburnum prized for its glossy, lustrous, dark green foliage that shows good resistance to the leaf spot diseases that can trouble arrowwood in humid climates, and for producing a heavier fruit set than the species, yielding abundant blue-black berries in fall that are an important food source for migrating and overwintering songbirds. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, drawing pollinators before the berries develop. It grows into a large, dense, multi-stemmed screening shrub with minimal maintenance once established, tolerating clay soil, urban conditions, and periodic drought. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Warren's Red Possumhaw Holly (Heavy-Fruiting Female Deciduous Holly for Winter Bird Food)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Warren's Red is a heavy-fruiting female selection of native deciduous holly, its persistent red berries a critical winter food source for cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds. Plant a male pollinator within range for fruit set.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a male possumhaw within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Warren's Red is one of the most widely planted and heaviest-fruiting selections of native possumhaw, or deciduous holly, dropping its leaves each fall to reveal branches absolutely laden with small, bright red berries that persist through much of winter, a dramatic and highly ornamental display in the bare-branch season when few other plants offer color. Those berries are a critical late-winter food source for cedar waxwings, American robins, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds, often stripped in a single flock visit once fully softened by cold. It tolerates a wide range of soils, including seasonally wet sites, and needs little maintenance once established. Prune to shape immediately after the fruit display fades, if needed.

common_name: Red Sprite Winterberry (Dwarf Compact Female Winterberry for Small Wildlife Gardens)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Sprite is a dwarf, compact female selection of native winterberry holly, only 3-5 feet tall, ideal for small gardens. Plant a compatible male pollinator within range for fruit set.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male winterberry within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Red Sprite is a genuine dwarf selection of native winterberry, staying just 3 to 5 feet tall at maturity, considerably smaller than most winterberry cultivars, making it one of the best choices for a small yard, foundation planting, or mixed border where a full-sized winterberry would be too large. Despite its compact size it produces a generous crop of bright red berries each fall that persist on the bare branches well into winter after the leaves drop, an important food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other birds during lean winter months. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs, making it useful in a rain garden or low spot. Prune to shape in late winter before new growth begins, if needed.

common_name: Winter Gold Winterberry (Rare Gold-Apricot-Berried Native Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Winter Gold bears unusual gold-to-apricot berries, distinct from the red-fruited winterberry cultivars more commonly grown. Plant a compatible male pollinator within range for fruit set.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male winterberry within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Winter Gold is a rare and distinctive winterberry selection bearing berries in a warm gold-to-apricot tone rather than the classic bright red of most cultivars, a striking, unusual color option that stands out in the winter landscape and in cut branches used for holiday arrangements. The berries persist on the bare branches well into winter after leaf drop, providing the same valuable food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other birds as red-fruited winterberry selections. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs, making it useful in a rain garden or low spot, and requires little routine care once established. Prune to shape in late winter before new growth begins, if needed.

common_name: Duet Variegated Beautyberry (First Stable Variegated White-Berried Beautyberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Duet, a 2006 US National Arboretum and Tennessee Tech release, is the first stable variegated-foliage beautyberry, bearing white-margined leaves and white berries that feed songbirds through winter.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Duet, released in 2006 through a collaboration between the U.S. National Arboretum and Tennessee Tech University, was the first stable variegated-foliage beautyberry introduced to cultivation, bearing leaves crisply edged in white that provide season-long ornamental interest well before the berries even form, on the same arching, graceful branches typical of purple beautyberry. In fall, the plant produces clusters of pure white berries along the stems rather than the more familiar violet-purple, a striking, luminous display against the variegated foliage, and those berries persist into winter as a valuable food source for mockingbirds, robins, and other songbirds. It performs best with a hard pruning in late winter, since it flowers and fruits on new growth, encouraging vigorous new stems each season. An outstanding dual-purpose foliage-and-fruit shrub for the wildlife or mixed border.

common_name: Jersey Princess American Holly (Premier Rutgers Dense Heavy-Fruiting Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jersey Princess, a Rutgers University release, is a premier female selection of native American holly with dense pyramidal form and a heavy, long-persisting crop of red berries. Plant a compatible male pollinator within range for fruit set.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male American holly within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Jersey Princess, bred and released by Rutgers University, is widely regarded as one of the finest American holly cultivars available, forming a dense, uniform, classically pyramidal evergreen tree clothed in glossy, spiny dark green leaves and producing an exceptionally heavy crop of bright red berries that persist on the tree for months into winter, a long-lasting food source for cedar waxwings, robins, mockingbirds, and other birds during the leanest part of the year. Its dense, tidy habit needs less corrective pruning than many holly cultivars to look its best. An outstanding evergreen specimen, screen, or wildlife tree for a Southern landscape with acidic soil.
